draft.title: Juries
card: A jury is a group of ordinary citizens who decide the facts in a criminal trial. In NSW, a jury of 12 is used in serious (indictable) trials in the higher courts.
The jury decides whether the accused is guilty or not guilty. The judge directs the jury on the law and runs the trial, but the jury decides guilt.
A jury is first asked to reach a unanimous verdict, where all 12 agree. If it cannot after long and genuine deliberation, the judge may accept a majority verdict in some cases.
In NSW, a majority verdict can be 11 to 1. The judge must be satisfied that the jury has deliberated for long enough and is unlikely to reach a unanimous verdict.
draft.remember: The jury of 12 decides guilt, and a judge may accept 11 to 1 in some cases.

a.q: In a serious NSW trial before a jury, who decides whether the accused is guilty?
opts: The judge who runs the trial
The defence lawyer for the accused
a.why: The jury decides the facts and reaches the verdict. The judge runs the trial and directs the jury on the law, which is why the judge is the most tempting wrong answer, but the judge does not decide guilt.
a.clue: Think about who weighs the evidence, not who runs the court.

b.q: After many hours, a NSW jury in a murder trial is split 11 to 1 for guilty. The judge is satisfied it has deliberated long enough and will not reach a unanimous verdict. What can the judge do?
opts: Order a retrial before a new jury
Enter a verdict of guilty without the jury
Direct the jury to stay until all 12 agree
b.why: NSW allows a majority verdict of 11 to 1 in some cases, once the judge is satisfied the jury is unlikely to reach a unanimous verdict. A retrial is not needed here, because the law allows the majority verdict to stand.
b.clue: The judge is satisfied that more time will not produce agreement.

check.summary: No problems found. The card matches the NSW Jury Act majority verdict rules, and both questions have one clearly right answer.
